title: Sequence Parallelism & Ring Attention: How Circular KV P2P Streaming Breaks the 1M+ Token Context Wall
summary: Scaling transformer context windows to hundreds of thousands or millions of tokens causes standard multi-head attention to collide with a brutal memory wall: activation tensors and Key-Value caches grow linearly or quadratically with sequence length, quickly exceeding the 80 GB VRAM limit of modern GPUs. Traditional Tensor Parallelism cannot solve this because it splits attention heads—capping parallelism at the head count and requiring latency-sensitive All-Reduce collectives across high-cost interconnects. Sequence Parallelism and Ring Attention solve this by sharding the sequence dimension across a logical ring of GPUs. By keeping Query tokens stationary on each device and continuously streaming Key-Value blocks to neighboring GPUs via non-blocking peer-to-peer transfers, Ring Attention overlaps network communication with matrix multiplication while using online softmax to assemble exact attention outputs across infinite context lengths.
analogyTitle: The Real-Life Analogy: The Circular Study Table vs. The 1,000-Page Photocopy Room
analogy:
Imagine a research team tasked with cross-referencing an enormous 1,000-page historical transcript against a set of complex forensic questions.

Under Classic Single-Device Processing (The Photocopy Room), one researcher tries to bring all 1,000 pages into their small office cubicle. Within minutes, stacks of paper fill the chairs, block the door, and bury the desk. The researcher collapses from cognitive overload—an Out of Memory (OOM) crash.

Under Tensor Parallelism (Splitting the Lenses), you hire 8 researchers, but instead of dividing the pages, you give all 8 workers the entire 1,000-page document and assign each person one tiny analytical question (e.g., Worker 1 checks dates, Worker 2 checks names). Every time anyone reads a single sentence, all 8 workers must stand up and shout their intermediate notes across the hall to stay synchronized. If you only have 8 questions, you can never add a 9th worker, and your hallway descends into shouting chaos.

Under Ring Attention (The Circular Study Table), you place 4 researchers around a circular table and divide the document into 250-page sections: Researcher 0 holds Pages 1–250, Researcher 1 holds Pages 251–500, and so on. Each researcher writes down their own questions (their Query slice) and keeps them stationary on their desk. In Round 1, they read the 250 pages in front of them (their local Key & Value). Then, in Round 2, each researcher slides their 250-page folder clockwise to their neighbor while receiving a folder from their counter-clockwise partner. While reading the newly arrived pages, they pass the previous stack along. After just 3 quick passes around the circle, every researcher has cross-checked their questions against every single page in the 1,000-page archive—without anyone ever having more than 250 pages on their desk at any given moment.

sections.heading: 1. The Context Length Memory Wall: Why Tensor Parallelism Fails on Long Sequences
sections.content:
In production large language models, the quest for long-context reasoning—analyzing entire code repositories, hours of audio, or hundreds of legal documents—runs straight into a physical hardware wall. When sequence length $S$ scales from standard 4,000 tokens to 128,000 or 1,000,000 tokens, memory consumption explodes across two dimensions:

• KV Cache Memory Footprint: For a model with $L$ layers, hidden dimension $d$, and batch size $B$, the Key and Value cache requires $2 \times 2 \times B \times S \times d \times L$ bytes in FP16 precision. For a 70B parameter model at $S = 128\text{K}$, the KV cache alone demands over 80 GB of memory—surpassing the total high-bandwidth memory (HBM) of an NVIDIA H100 GPU before loading a single weight parameter or activation tensor.
• Intermediate Attention Maps: Standard self-attention computes the scaled dot-product attention score $A = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V$. The intermediate score matrix $Q K^T$ requires $O(S^2)$ memory. At $S = 1\text{M}$, a single attention head requires an uncompressed float matrix of $10^{12}$ elements—or 2 Terabytes of VRAM per head!

While algorithms like FlashAttention tile the computation into fast on-chip SRAM to avoid materializing the $O(S^2)$ matrix in HBM, FlashAttention still assumes that the complete input tensors $Q$, $K$, and $V$ fit within the memory of a single physical device.

When engineers try to scale context length using traditional Tensor Parallelism (TP) (such as Megatron-LM), they hit two fatal architectural boundaries:

1. Bounded by KV Head Count: Tensor parallelism shards linear projection matrices across attention heads. In modern architectures utilizing Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)—like Llama 3 with only 8 KV heads—TP cannot exceed a degree of 8. You cannot add a 16th or 32nd GPU to handle a longer prompt.
2. Intra-Node Communication Bottlenecks: Tensor parallelism requires two blocking All-Reduce collectives per transformer layer. Over high-speed intra-node NVLink (900 GB/s), this is fast; but spanning TP across nodes over 400 Gbps InfiniBand causes communication latency to dominate, bringing compute utilization to a dead crawl.

sections.heading: 2. Sequence Parallelism Paradigms: DeepSpeed Ulysses vs. Ring Attention
sections.content:
To scale beyond the single-GPU context limit, engineers turn to Sequence Parallelism (SP), which partitions the sequence dimension $S$ rather than the hidden dimension or batch size. Two leading paradigms define modern sequence-parallel architectures:

• DeepSpeed Ulysses (All-to-All Sequence Parallelism):
Ulysses shards the input token sequence evenly across $N$ GPUs: each GPU holds an $S/N$ token slice across all attention heads. Before computing self-attention, Ulysses performs an All-to-All collective communication primitive. This transposes the tensor layout from sequence-sharded with all heads to head-sharded with full sequence length ($S$). Each GPU computes standard local FlashAttention on its assigned subset of heads across the full sequence, followed by a second All-to-All to transpose back.

While elegant and performant within high-bandwidth clusters, Ulysses shares Tensor Parallelism's fundamental constraint: the degree of sequence parallelism $N$ cannot exceed the total number of attention heads $H$. For models with few KV heads, Ulysses cannot scale to massive clusters.

• Ring Attention (Hao Liu, Matei Zaharia, Pieter Abbeel, 2023):
Ring Attention eliminates the head-count constraint and the costly global All-to-All collective entirely. Instead, it arranges $N$ GPUs into a logical circular ring ($0 \to 1 \to 2 \dots \to N-1 \to 0$).

1. Partitioning: The sequence of length $S$ is divided into $N$ equal chunks of size $B = S/N$. GPU $i$ holds the $i$-th chunk of Query ($Q_i$), Key ($K_i$), and Value ($V_i$) vectors.
2. Stationary Queries: Throughout the entire attention calculation of the layer, the Query block $Q_i$ remains stationary in GPU $i$'s local memory.
3. P2P Ring Circulation: The Key and Value blocks are passed along the ring in a continuous pipeline of non-blocking peer-to-peer point-to-point transfers (MPI_Isend / MPI_Irecv or NCCL sendrecv).
4. Step-by-Step Execution:
• Step 0: GPU $i$ computes block attention between its stationary $Q_i$ and its local $K_i, V_i$. Simultaneously, it initiates an asynchronous P2P transfer of $K_i, V_i$ to GPU $(i+1) \pmod N$ and begins receiving $K_{i-1}, V_{i-1}$ from GPU $(i-1) \pmod N$.
• Step 1: Once the transfer completes, GPU $i$ computes block attention between $Q_i$ and the newly received $K_{i-1}, V_{i-1}$, while concurrently passing that block along to the next device.
• After $N-1$ steps: Every Query token on every GPU has attended to every Key-Value token in the global sequence, with zero device ever holding more than $1/N$ of the total context.

sections.heading: 3. The Secret Sauce: Online Softmax Rescaling & Complete Compute-Communication Overlap
sections.content:
The mathematical genius of Ring Attention lies in two critical mechanisms: Online Softmax Rescaling and Zero-Bubble Latency Overlapping.

• The Online Softmax Challenge:
Softmax is inherently non-local: computing $\text{softmax}(x)_i = \frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_j e^{x_j}}$ requires knowledge of the global maximum and the global denominator across all keys. If keys arrive in sequential chunks across ring steps, how can a GPU compute exact attention outputs without waiting for all keys to arrive?

Ring Attention integrates the online softmax formula popularized by FlashAttention. Each GPU maintains three running accumulators in registers:
• $m^{(k)}$: The running maximum attention score across all blocks processed up to step $k$.
• $\ell^{(k)}$: The running denominator (sum of exponents) up to step $k$.
• $O^{(k)}$: The running unnormalized output accumulator.

When a new block of keys $K_{new}$ and values $V_{new}$ arrives in step $k+1$, the GPU computes local score block $S = Q_i K_{new}^T / \sqrt{d_k}$ and finds its local maximum $\tilde{m}$. It computes the new global maximum $m^{(k+1)} = \max(m^{(k)}, \tilde{m})$. It then rescales the existing accumulator: $O^{(k+1)} = O^{(k)} \cdot e^{m^{(k)} - m^{(k+1)}} + P_{new} V_{new}$, where $P_{new} = e^{S - m^{(k+1)}}$. This allows the running attention output to be updated incrementally with bitwise numerical equivalence to global full-sequence attention!

• Why Communication Overhead Approaches Zero:
In distributed systems, network latency kills scaling. However, in Ring Attention, as sequence length increases, the arithmetic intensity works overwhelmingly in the engineer's favor:

• Computation Complexity: Computing block matrix multiplication between $Q_i \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times d}$ and $K_j \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times d}$ scales quadratically with block size: $O(B^2 \cdot d)$ FLOPs.
• Communication Complexity: Transferring $K_j$ and $V_j$ between ring neighbors scales linearly with block size: $O(B \cdot d)$ bytes.

Because computation grows as $O(B^2)$ while communication only grows as $O(B)$, setting the block size $B = S/N$ sufficiently large (typically $\ge 4\text{K}$ tokens) ensures that the time to compute the GEMM on NVIDIA Tensor Cores is significantly longer than the time required to transfer the next block over inter-GPU networking. By running communication on a background CUDA stream, the network transfer is 100% hidden behind computation, achieving zero communication bubbles.

• Causal Zig-Zag Ring Attention:
In causal (autoregressive) models, tokens cannot attend to future positions ($t' > t$). In a naive ring layout, nearly half of the blocks would be completely masked out, leaving GPUs idle. Modern implementations utilize Zig-Zag Block Striping: instead of assigning contiguous sequence chunks, tokens are striped across GPUs (e.g., interleaving front and back halves of the sequence). This ensures that every GPU across all ring steps processes an identical volume of non-masked causal tokens, maintaining 100% load balance across the cluster.

takeaway: Context length scaling in modern language models is fundamentally constrained by single-GPU VRAM limits and the quadratic attention memory wall. Sequence Parallelism overcomes this bottleneck by distributing the sequence dimension across cluster nodes. While DeepSpeed Ulysses relies on heavy All-to-All collective communication bounded by attention head count, Ring Attention organizes GPUs into a circular pipeline where local Query blocks remain stationary while Key-Value blocks circulate continuously via non-blocking peer-to-peer transfers. By leveraging online softmax rescaling to update partial attention accumulators on-the-fly and overlapping linear network communication behind quadratic matrix multiplication, Ring Attention eliminates communication bubbles and unlocks million-token context windows across distributed GPU clusters.
